explanations.answer: Carry on business and make a profit
explanations.explanation: That's the plan, baker. They say they'll spend a year in some city, carry on business and make a profit (James 4:13). Notice what's missing: not one word about asking the Lord first. A year of business, all mapped out, and nobody checked who owns the calendar.

explanations.answer: Build a house and settle down there
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The planners say they'll spend a year there, and the plan is to "…carry on business, and make a profit." (James 4:13). Building a house isn't in what they say. Their plan is business and profit, and I bet they had the spreadsheet already open.

explanations.answer: Visit family and rest for a while
explanations.explanation: I wish it were a vacation, baker, but it's not. The planners say they'll go to this or that city, spend a year there, carry on business and make a profit (James 4:13). Visiting family and resting isn't in what they say. Their plan is business and profit.

Careful, friend, it's the opposite. James tells them, "You do not even know what will happen tomorrow!" (James 4:14). They talk like they've already read the last page of next year, and James says they haven't even read tomorrow. That's a big gap between a plan and a promise.

That's right, baker. James says the exact opposite: "You do not even know what will happen tomorrow!" (James 4:14). The planners sound sure about a whole year, but they can't see past the next sunrise. I know that feeling, because I've had tomorrow flip on me without warning.

That's it, baker. James says, "You are a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes." (James 4:14). A mist shows up, hangs around a bit and is gone. Short, quiet and over before you can set a timer.

Nice picture, friend, but that's a different passage. A tree planted by water is how Psalm 1:3 describes the one who delights in the Lord's law. Here James calls life "…a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes." (James 4:14). Trees stay put, and mist does not.

Whoa, friend, that's the opposite of what James says. He calls life "…a mist that appears for a little while and then vanishes." (James 4:14). A rock sits there and never moves, and a mist is gone after a little while. Nothing about this picture is solid.

Yes, baker. James says they ought to say, "If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that." (James 4:15). Plans aren't banned. He just wants the Lord in them. Make the plan, hold it loosely and let Him have the last word.

Good guess, friend, but not the word. James says, "If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that." (James 4:15). Willing, not watching. It's about whose say-so the plan rests on, not just who's looking on while we make it.

Not the word, friend. James says, "If the Lord is willing, we will live and do this or that." (James 4:15). It's about the Lord's will over our plans. Even the plan to bake a batch tomorrow rests on that, friend.
Right, baker, and James doesn't soften it: "All such boasting is evil." (James 4:16). Boasting in proud intentions means acting like tomorrow belongs to you. That's a strong word, and he means it.
Oh, friend, no. James says the opposite: "All such boasting is evil." (James 4:16). He's talking about boasting in proud intentions. Calling it wise would be like calling a burnt batch a masterpiece.
I'd love that to be true, baker, but James says, "All such boasting is evil." (James 4:16). He doesn't treat it as a small slip. Boasting in proud intentions is serious to him, so he says so plainly.

That's right, baker. James says, "Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do, yet fails to do it, is guilty of sin." (James 4:17). It isn't only about doing wrong things. Knowing the good thing and skipping it counts too. That one makes me stop and think.

That sounds kind, friend, but it's not what James writes. He says, "Anyone, then, who knows the right thing to do, yet fails to do it, is guilty of sin." (James 4:17). The key is that they already know. Learning isn't the issue when the right thing is sitting right there.

Not here, baker. James says that anyone who knows the right thing to do and fails to do it "…is guilty of sin." (James 4:17). Knowing and not doing leaves no blame-free zone. It's a short line, but it lands hard.

That's the word, baker. James says, "…weep and wail over the misery to come upon you." (James 5:1). He's talking to the rich, and he doesn't start with a pat on the back. Misery is coming, and he tells them to weep over it.

Not this time, friend. James tells the rich to "…weep and wail over the misery to come upon you." (James 5:1). Singing would be a party, and this is no party. Misery is on the way, so the song will have to wait.
Nice thought, baker, but no naps here. James says, "…weep and wail over the misery to come upon you." (James 5:1). There's misery coming for the rich, and he wants them to weep, not recline.

Yes, baker. James says, "Your riches have rotted and moths have eaten your clothes." (James 5:2). Fine clothes in the closet, and moths made lunch of them. I think that's a hard way to find out what stored-up stuff is worth.

Not thieves, friend. James says, "Your riches have rotted and moths have eaten your clothes." (James 5:2). Thieves aren't mentioned in this verse. The moths are the ones who ate the clothes, which is a quiet kind of loss.
Good guess, baker, but rain isn't what James names. He says, "…moths have eaten your clothes." (James 5:2). The damage he points to comes from moths. Rain doesn't show up in this verse.

Careful, friend, James says the reverse. He writes, "Your gold and silver are corroded." (James 5:3). Gold and silver that are corroded aren't shining like new. That's the opposite of the picture in the question.
That's right, baker. James says, "Your gold and silver are corroded." (James 5:3). Nothing shiny about it. Treasure sitting in storage ends up looking like the bottom of a very old pan.

Yes, baker. James says, "Their corrosion will testify against you and consume your flesh like fire." (James 5:3). The rust itself speaks up like a witness. A pile of treasure left sitting has a lot to say.

If only, friend, but no. James says, "Their corrosion will testify against you…" (James 5:3). Paying off debts isn't what he says it will do. The corrosion becomes a witness against the ones who hoarded the treasure.

Not quite, baker. James says, "Their corrosion will testify against you and consume your flesh like fire." (James 5:3). The corrosion doesn't guard a thing. It stands up and speaks against the people who stashed the treasure.
That's it, baker. James says, "…the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields…" (James 5:4). The workers mowed the fields, and their wages were withheld. I think that stings.

Good guess, friend, but water isn't what James names. He says, "…the wages you withheld from the workmen who mowed your fields…" (James 5:4). It was their pay held back. The workers did the mowing and went without what they earned.
Not tools, baker. James says the rich withheld "the wages" from the workmen who mowed their fields (James 5:4). Tools aren't mentioned in the verse. What was held back was their pay.

That's right, baker. James says, "The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts." (James 5:4). The harvesters may have felt unheard, but their cries got through. I take comfort that He hears every one.
Other way around, friend. James says, "The cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts." (James 5:4). Their cries reached Him. That makes the statement true, not false.

Yes, baker. James says, "You have lived on earth in luxury and self-indulgence." (James 5:5). Comfort and indulgence were the daily menu. That's a sharp contrast with the harvesters waiting on their pay.

Close, friend, but not the word. James says, "You have lived on earth in luxury and self-indulgence." (James 5:5). Luxury is the word he uses for how they lived. Hardship isn't the word in this verse.

Nope, baker. James says, "You have lived on earth in luxury and self-indulgence." (James 5:5). Silence isn't the word he uses. Luxury is, and it comes right after the cries of the harvesters in the verse before.

Hold on, friend, James says the opposite. He says the rich "…have condemned and murdered the righteous, who did not resist you." (James 5:6). The righteous didn't fight back. I think this is one of the heavy parts of the letter.

Right, baker. James says the righteous "…did not resist you." (James 5:6). They didn't fight back against those who condemned and murdered them. I think this is a heavy verse, and it deserves a quiet moment.
